rationale: The book's entry makes a modest, well-evidenced lexical-theological claim: 'works' names deeds as such, a semantically neutral term whose moral and soteriological valence is supplied by context — the command a deed executes (making it obedience or disobedience) and whether a wage is claimed for it (Paul's actual target in Romans 4). Every element of the printed entry is directly carried by its cited texts: Exodus 18:20 defines 'the work that they must do' where the law is first taught; Micah 6:16 shows evil 'works' as deeds executing the wrong commands (the statutes of Omri, the works of the house of Ahab); Psalm 111:7 pairs God's works with His commandments; Luke 17:7-10 establishes that even complete obedience creates no wage-claim; Romans 4:4-5 explicitly frames the excluded 'work' in wage/debt vocabulary; James 2:21-22 shows the same word naming faith's visible enactment. The strongest rival — the Lutheran/Reformed polemical reading in which Pauline 'works' inherently means human obedience or self-effort opposed to grace — cannot account for Luke 17:10 (where commanded obedience is required yet earns nothing, exactly the duty/wage distinction the book draws), for Ephesians 2:10 and Titus 3:8 (works commanded immediately after being excluded), or for Revelation 2:26 (works 'kept' like commandments). The book explains the whole distribution of the term with one neutral referent plus stated contextual modifiers; the counter must posit a shifting, context-dependent negative freight it never derives from the texts. Note also that the common interpretation itself concedes the core (works = deeds), so much of the apparent divergence concerns mechanism rather than referent; where genuine contradiction exists (works-as-inherent-self-righteousness), the book wins on the evidence.
book_core_identification: A 'work' is a deed or action as such — not a synonym for obedience and not an inherently negative cipher for self-righteous effort. The deed becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command and disobedience when the deed or its commanding authority conflicts with God's command; and no work, not even complete obedience, creates a wage-claim on God (Luke 17:10), which is the specific claim Paul excludes in Romans 4:4-5 while James 2 uses the same word for faith's visible enactment.
book_secondary_elaborations: The occurrence-by-occurrence classification of Paul's 'works of the law' phrases (God's law vs. circumcision-party application vs. ambiguous) in The End of the Law
The telos/purpose reading of Romans 10:4 and the broader continuity claims about the law (feast, new moon, sabbath in Colossians 2; Romans 14; Acts 15)
The wage/debt economic analysis as the uniform key to all of Paul's 'not of works' statements (Rom 9:11; 2 Tim 1:9; Titus 3:5)
The integration with the four-offices scheme (love, knowing, faith, belief) in chapter 6, in which works are the commandment-shaped enactment of trust
The textual note on Romans 9:32 (TR 'works of the law' vs. critical text 'as if by works')
strongest_counter_interpretation: The Lutheran/Reformed polemical reading (Response A, alternative 3): in Paul's soteriological usage, 'works' is not a neutral word for deeds but shorthand for autonomous human effort and self-righteousness — man's attempt to earn standing with God apart from Christ. On this reading Paul's exclusion of works excludes human obedience as such from any role in justification, drawing on Romans 4:4-5, Romans 9:32 and 11:6, Philippians 3:9, Titus 3:5, and Isaiah 64:6 ('all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags'). Works therefore carries intrinsic negative soteriological freight in Paul, and the good-works passages belong to a separate, post-justification register.
counter_core_identification: 'Works' in Paul's exclusionary contexts denotes human moral effort and obedience offered as a basis of standing with God — an inherently grace-opposed category — rather than a neutral term for deeds whose status is fixed by command and wage-claim.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that 'works' is a neutral deed-word: it holds that in Pauline soteriology the term itself names obedience-as-merit, so that human obedience as such — not merely the wage-claim attached to it — is what Paul excludes; the book's claim that Romans 4 sets faith against labor-for-wages rather than against obedience would then misidentify Paul's target.
counter_case: Romans 4:4-5 read as excluding the worker per se, not merely his wage-claim
Romans 11:6 — 'if by grace, then it is no more of works' as a categorical antithesis
Philippians 3:9 — Paul renounces 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law'
Titus 3:5 — 'not by works of righteousness which we have done'
Isaiah 64:6 — human righteousness itself as filthy rags, suggesting works are intrinsically disqualified
The reading's simplicity: one fixed negative referent for 'works' in every justification context
book_explanatory_advantages: Luke 17:7-10, printed with the entry, is decisive: the servant's deeds are commanded, performed, and commended as duty, yet earn no wage — proving that what Paul excludes is the wage-claim (Rom 4:4 'reckoned... of debt'), not obedience itself, since obedience here is required while creating no debt

Romans 4:4 uses explicit economic vocabulary (worketh, reward, reckoned, grace, debt) that the book's laborer-for-wages reading takes at face value; the counter must treat this vocabulary as incidental to a broader anti-obedience polemic it does not state

Exodus 18:20, Psalm 111:7, and Micah 6:16 show 'works' functioning as a neutral deed-word across good and evil uses — commanded work, God's own works paired with His commandments, and Ahab's works executing rival statutes — exactly the command-relative definition the entry gives
James 2:21-22 is explained without tension: the same word names Abraham's deed as faith made visible, no wage claimed; the counter must quarantine James from Paul or subordinate one to the other

Ephesians 2:8-10's dual movement (not of works / created unto good works) follows naturally: works excluded as purchase price, restored as the life the gift creates — the counter's intrinsically negative 'works' makes verse 10's immediate commendation of the same word awkward
Revelation 2:26 ('keepeth my works') and Titus 3:5 with 3:8 ('maintain good works') show the word governed by context and possessor, not by fixed negative freight
Paul's own summary in Romans 3:31 ('we establish the law') fits the book's account of what is and is not excluded
counter_explanatory_advantages: Offers a single, simple referent for 'works' in every Pauline justification text, requiring no context-by-context adjudication
Coheres with Isaiah 64:6 and Philippians 3:9, where human righteousness itself is disparaged, and with a long confessional tradition of reading Paul this way
Guards more starkly against any synergistic inference from the book's claim that obedience is not what Paul excludes
decisive_sources: Luke 17:7-10 (KJV excerpt supplied) — commanded obedience performed in full yet yielding no wage, establishing duty vs. wages as the operative distinction
Romans 4:4-5 (KJV excerpt supplied) — the excluded work defined by its economic claim ('reward... of debt')
Exodus 18:20 (KJV excerpt supplied) — 'the work that they must do' defined where the law is first taught
Micah 6:16 (KJV excerpt supplied) — evil works as deeds executing rival statutes, proving the command-relative valence of the word
James 2:21-22 (KJV excerpt supplied) — the same word naming faith's visible, wage-free enactment
Ephesians 2:8-10 and Titus 3:5, 8 as treated in The End of the Law — works excluded as purchase price, immediately commanded as fruit
Psalm 111:7 (KJV excerpt supplied) — God's works and commandments as two halves of one line
unresolved_objections: The companion chapter's occurrence-classification of 'works of the law' and its broader continuity claims (feasts, sabbath, Colossians 2, Romans 14, Acts 15) exceed the entry's core and remain individually contestable; they are not needed for, and were not adjudicated as part of, the core identification

The New Perspective reading (works of the law as covenant boundary markers) is only partially engaged; the book concedes context-dependence for erga nomou but its Galatians 2 classification could be disputed without touching the core
The book's confidence that Romans 4's wage-frame governs all of Paul's 'not of works' statements (e.g., 2 Tim 1:9, Rom 9:11) is an extension the entry's own citations do not fully prove
Whether 'not a synonym for obedience' understates a genuinely polemical edge in some Pauline uses (Rom 9:32) remains a live, non-decisive question
